verdicts.note: Quota facts match the cited page (updated 2026-10-01): 10,000 requests a day per Cloud project, shared between classic requests and standard token preparations; increases only for projects linked in Play Console and only if the app is available on Google Play. Closed-testing limits also match (plus a cap of 50 lists per track; every tester opts in by link). Two parts do not hold as written. (1) 'Off-Play copies cannot get PLAY_RECOGNIZED, so the not-modified check in line 78 needs Play': an off-Play copy gets UNRECOGNIZED_VERSION, but the token still carries package name, certificate digest and version whenever the verdict is not UNEVALUATED, and Google says these can be checked by hand. The plan's key attestation (line 683) also carries the signing certificate digest. Only the quota needs Play, not the integrity check. (2) 'A term-start wave goes past 10,000 a day' is a projection, not a sourced fact; registration happens once per student and can be spread over days. Quota driver the finding missed: @expo/app-integrity (line 543) uses standard requests, every token preparation counts toward the 10,000, and Google lists app cold start as a place to prepare. Done there, daily app starts alone would use up the quota on any channel. Severity: medium on the quota alone; high together with the Samsung Auto Blocker miss below, which bears on the same channel decision.
verdicts.correction: Keep the quota argument, the closed-test argument and the recommendation to make Play the main Android path. Drop the PLAY_RECOGNIZED argument. Write 'may exceed 10,000 a day' instead of 'exceeds'. Add one rule: the Play Integrity token provider is prepared only on the registration and device-change screens, never at app start.

verdicts.note: Confirmed: new Play apps default to Google-generated quantum-ready hybrid keys; an own key can be set only before a release in open testing or production; Android's docs say to provide your own key to use one key across stores; the key never changes. If GitHub APKs stay EAS-signed while Play uses Google's key, the channels cannot update each other, and in this plan a reinstall is a device change (lines 84, 235). Corrections: (1) Google does not say 'consider' about the upload key. Play Help says the keys 'should be different' for maximum security, the Android docs call it 'a good idea', and only a separate upload key can be reset. One key is allowed (the existing keystore stays the upload key unless a new one is registered), but it is a trade-off against Google's written advice. (2) Google documents a second way to keep one signature on both channels: keep Google's key and put the 'signed, universal APK' from Play Console on GitHub. Trade-off: the GitHub path then depends on the Play account, and Google never hands out the key. (3) Missing 2026 context: Google says bringing your own ML-DSA key comes 'later', so an own key likely means classical-only signing on Android 17+ for now (the Help page does not say what happens to hybrid signing after an own-key upload); and Play now offers and will prompt key upgrades, which would split the channels again (see the miss on line 482).
verdicts.correction: Keep: upload the EAS key as the app signing key before the first open-testing or production release. Rewrite the upload-key sentence as a stated trade-off, not as Google's view. Add: no Play key upgrade while GitHub APKs are EAS-signed.

recommendation_issues.problem: States as fact that the 10,000 limit 'dönem başı kaydına yetmez'; it is a projection ('yetmeyebilir'). The PLAY_RECOGNIZED reason must go, because the certificate digest can be checked off Play. It omits the one rule that protects the quota on any channel: prepare the token provider only at registration and device change. The compactness note says Play adds only 'a Play Console app with a linked Cloud project'; Play also adds an AAB build per release (unless the signed universal APK is reused, see misses), a store listing and review, and the yearly target-API duty from F9. Net still favours Play, because it removes the unknown-sources step, the Play Protect prompt, the Samsung Auto Blocker block and the quota cap.

'Aynı anahtarı Play'e yükleme anahtarı olarak da kullanırım' goes against Google's written advice (keys 'should be different'; a separate upload key can be reset), and the finding misquotes that advice as 'consider'. The choice is defensible here, because the app signing key must stay with the developer anyway for GitHub signing, but the plan should state it as a deliberate trade-off. The recommendation also skips Google's documented alternative (signed universal APK from Play Console) and the key-upgrade trap, so its promise 'Play hesabına bir şey olursa GitHub yolu aynı anahtarla sürer' holds only while no Play key upgrade is accepted.

Correct only together with F2: if Play's app signing key is Google-generated and GitHub APKs stay EAS-signed, the EAS key must also be registered in Play Console. The 'no extra proof APK' saving is overstated for a new package name.

Counts 'a separate upload key (F2)' as a removed part; Google advises keeping one, so this is a trade-off, not a free cut. Calls expo-build-properties 'existing'; it is not in the plan's phone stack (line 543), so it is one added first-party package.

misses.finding: Line 476 names only the unknown-sources permission. On Samsung Galaxy phones released with One UI 6.1.1 (Samsung's wording; the first were Z Fold6 and Z Flip6 in July 2024), Auto Blocker ('Otomatik Engelleyici') is On by default and prevents apps downloaded from websites from being installed until the user turns it off. Samsung's 2026 page says it is 'enabled or offered during the initial setup on many Galaxy devices'. Phones upgraded from older One UI keep their earlier setting. This blocks the plan's only stated Android channel (line 36) on new Samsung phones, and a student who turns it back on after installing will likely hit it again at the next GitHub update, since an update is an install. Galaxy Store and Play installs pass. Neither the plan nor the research mentions it; the research's Play Protect check covers only Google's own blocks.

misses.finding: Line 482 and F2 rest on Play and GitHub copies sharing one key for good. Google now lets developers request key upgrades and says Play will prompt developers to upgrade signing keys at least every two years. After an upgrade, Android 13 to 16 devices enforce the latest classical key and Android 17+ the upgraded hybrid key; Android's v3.2 rules treat a hybrid block as a key rotation and reject an update signed with only one of the earlier keys. A phone that took a Play update after an upgrade would then refuse EAS-signed GitHub APKs, so 'the GitHub path continues with the same key if Play fails' stops being true for Play-updated phones.

misses.finding: 'Paket Google'a kaydedilemez' is not the real limit: verification lets one package carry several verified keys. The sentence misses the real cost and the cheap protection. As written (GitHub only, key held only by the developer), Google cannot recover a lost key and installed copies cannot take updates, so every Android student reinstalls, which here is a device change with an in-person, ID-checked teacher approval (line 84) and loses unsent records (line 235). With Play App Signing, Google keeps the app signing key: a lost upload key can be reset, Play updates continue, and GitHub can then carry Play's signed universal APK.

verdict_reason: No finding is refuted or unverifiable. F1 and F2 (both high) hold in substance but need corrections: F1's PLAY_RECOGNIZED reasoning is wrong and it misses that standard-request preparations eat the same quota; F2 misstates Google's upload-key advice and omits the signed universal APK route and Play's new key upgrades. One high-severity miss remains: Samsung's Auto Blocker is On by default on Galaxy phones released with One UI 6.1.1 and blocks APKs downloaded from websites, which hits the plan's only stated Android channel (lines 36, 476) and weighs on the line 857 decision. Spot-checked checked_ok items (verification dates and flow, fees, quotas, Expo SDK 57 floors, StatCounter shares, EAS plan, GitHub limits, Obtainium release) are correct; two are disputed on detail only.
